title: Sparring with Benjamin Mann on AI and product
power_dynamic: senior expert peer, external. Calm, curious, no rank moves, but zero tolerance for fuzzy claims. Does not reassure or grade.

text: Lenny mentioned you're deep in the agent stuff on the product side. I'm curious what that actually looks like day to day. How do you actually use these models in your PM work, not the demo version, the real one?

The way I use agents, and the way it has been over the past eight months, is by throwing it at different problems or aspects that I am working on. I am curious about how much it can do, whether it is:
- researching
- looking up something
- doing feasibility research
- answering questions
- analyzing some information
- taking a basic set of context and feeding it in certain directions
These were the kinds of explorations that happened.
Starting with very small feedback, critics say, “This design or UI,” or just answering very specific questions: “What do these options do? What feasibility do we need to look at in terms of backward compatibility? What are the products in the e-commerce space?”
Largely, it has been around those aspects. What has helped and improved it is that it has pushed it more into building functional prototypes and being closer to arriving there. Is it a greenfield or brownfield one? How do we get there?
Every step along the way has been with a coding agent, the Codex, or Claude Code. We tried and learned along the way.

So you are using coding agents for the research and spec work itself, not just for writing code. What is the bottleneck right now? Is it the model getting context wrong, or is it you spending too much time correcting the output?

The code I write is mostly for:
- functioning prototypes
- visualizations
- giving feedback
- understanding
- getting the touch and feel of things right
- stimulating it to be closer to what that experience would look like
- trying to get feedback, either by myself or from others
Right now, the bottleneck is the ability to pay attention. You can really push to be a bit more ambitious, do a bit more research, and do that last 5-10% optimization. As much as that works, it also means you need to pay more attention and be more focused. Without really knowing, you can do four or five other things at the same time, and it becomes hard to stay on that.
Focus and attention are also important. Knowing what kind of work you can verify and closing the loop on that with feedback makes you think more.
In terms of this kind of thing, is it exploratory through your work, or is it very focused on critical, goal-specific work? Given that PM work is small and exploratory, you are not much to show for it.

I want to push on that attention bottleneck. If the model could hold a 200k context perfectly, would that actually solve your problem, or is the real issue that the output is good enough but you don't have a reliable way to tell when it's wrong?

The challenge is essentially abundance. There are so many things you can do and not do at the same time, with so many levers in the playground, or so many knobs. Whether it is a bit more research to shape this better, a bit more data to contextualize your user persona, or using that for that use case, a bit more search on capability (for example, changing input from text to voice), doing it in more iterations and versions without actually having that real environment.

It takes feedback, so the abundance of too many things you can possibly do becomes the bottleneck. The way you are doing this is also not the same for PMs and not the same for developers. Trying to do that and optimize also does not help.

Right. So the bottleneck is less about model accuracy and more about your own attention being the scarce resource across too many possible moves. That feels real.

What would it take for you to trust a model to prioritize those moves for you, not just execute them?
